title: The evening examen
hookLine: where was God today? where did I love? where did I fail?
tomorrow: what deadline does the Bible put on anger?

lines: OR I JUDGE NOT MINE OWN SELF?
cards: Lying in bed, the day on a loop: what you said, what you should have said, what they meant by that. Paul seems to point two ways about it.
To the church at Corinth he writes, “Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves.”
And in his earlier letter to the same church: “yea, I judge not mine own self,” because “he that judgeth me is the Lord.” So which is it? Look hard at your day, or hand the judging over?

teach.b: Christians keep both lines, and they lean differently. One side builds a nightly habit on the first. Ignatius of Loyola wrote a short review of the day into his Spiritual Exercises: the examen.
Its best case: a day nobody looks at tends to repeat itself, and God may have been in it unnoticed. Three questions carry it. Where was God today?
Where did I love? Where did I fail?

teach.h: SEEN ON THE REPLAY, LIKE EMMAUS.
teach.b: Luke's Emmaus story shows why looking back works. Two disciples realize only afterward, “Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?” They saw it on the replay.

teach.h: THE WORRY: A COURTROOM AT NIGHT.
teach.b: For some Christians, a nightly self-review can slide into anxious scorekeeping, a courtroom in the head every night. Their best case is Paul's own: I judge not mine own self; the Lord does. Hand it over and rest.
Here's where they meet. Ignatius's examen doesn't start with failures. It starts with thanks for this particular day's gifts, and it ends by asking pardon and looking to tomorrow.

teach.h: THANKS FIRST: A REVIEW, NOT A TRIAL.

teach.b: Both sides agree the day belongs to God. They differ on how closely to read it.

how: Christians who pray the examen take a few minutes, often at night: thanks for the day, a walk back through its hours, a request for pardon, and a look toward tomorrow; others end the day simply by handing it to God.

o: confessing your sins aloud to a priest at night
a written test at the end of a religion class
a short look back over the day, starting with thanks

games.q: two lines from Paul, and a nightly habit — tap the pairs.
p: he that judgeth me is the Lord
wrote the examen into his Exercises
did not our heart burn within us

s: the examen starts by listing your failures
Ignatius starts with thanks for the day's gifts.
Paul writes both examine yourselves and I judge not mine own self
two letters, to the same church at Corinth.

games.q: your friend skips any nightly review: "Paul says I judge not mine own self." state the examen side at its best.
o: God only forgives the faults you've listed and counted each night.
looking back with thanks shows where God was, like Emmaus on the replay.
everyone has to do the examen, or the day doesn't count.
games.why: the examen's best case: Emmaus seen afterward, and Paul's own examine yourselves. the other side's best case: the Lord judges, so rest. Ignatius starts with thanks.

practice: Count on your fingers three good things from today, small ones included: a joke, a meal, a message. Then walk the hours back from now to waking and ask the three questions once each, without holding court.
If you pray, end by handing the day over; if not, end where you began, on the thanks.

wordCard.voice: The evening examen. A short review of the day at night: thanks first, then where was God, where did I love, where did I fail.

orig.note: Latin (and Spanish): the name for this review of the day.

carryVoice: Your line: where was he? Asked after the thanks, it's a replay, not a trial. Good night for now.
